title: Given candidates that may contain duplicates and a target, return all unique combinations summing to target, where each candidate may be used at most once.
shortTitle: Combination Sum II — each number used once, skip duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: Sort the candidates, then backtrack advancing the start index by one each step so no element is reused, with a same-level duplicate skip (i > start and cand[i] == cand[i-1]) to avoid duplicate combinations. Record when the remaining target is zero and prune on overshoot.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India issues one-time cashback coupons, some of identical value, and a customer can use each coupon only once. To list every distinct set of coupons that reaches a target, you consume each coupon at most once and avoid listing the same-valued coupon twice at the same choice point.
s1_definition.oneliner: Advance index by one (use-once) and skip same-level duplicates to get unique combinations from a multiset.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sort the candidates, then backtrack advancing the start index by one each step so no element is reused, with a same-level duplicate skip (i > start and cand[i] == cand[i-1]) to avoid duplicate combinations. Record when the remaining target is zero and prune on overshoot.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India issues one-time cashback coupons, some of identical value, and a customer can use each coupon only once. To list every distinct set of coupons that reaches a target, you consume each coupon at most once and avoid listing the same-valued coupon twice at the same choice point.

**One line to remember:** Advance index by one (use-once) and skip same-level duplicates to get unique combinations from a multiset.

sections.s2_technical:
Sort so duplicates are adjacent. In the loop, skip a same-level duplicate, subtract the candidate, and recurse with `i+1` so the element is not reused. For example: `if (i>start && cand[i]==cand[i-1]) continue; path.add(cand[i]); backtrack(i+1, remain-cand[i]);`.

Advancing to `i+1` enforces use-once, distinguishing this from Combination Sum where the same index was reused. The duplicate skip ensures that identical values at the same level produce the combination only once.

Sorting also enables the `cand[i] > remain` break for pruning. The time is exponential in the worst case, well pruned on realistic inputs. A senior nuance is that the use-once rule plus the duplicate skip together handle the classic coin-collection-from-a-multiset problem cleanly, which is why this template is worth memorizing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a customer holds a wallet of one-time cashback coupons, some with identical values, and wants every distinct set of coupons that redeems to exactly a target. This is exactly how Combination Sum II works.

Problem 2 — Each coupon is consumed once and two identical coupons must not create two identical-looking sets. This is exactly why the index advances by one and same-level duplicates are skipped.

The mini-project builds a `CouponRedemptionPlanner`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The coupons sort to one, one, two, five, six, seven, ten with target eight.

Step 1: [1,7] sums to eight and is recorded using the first one.

Step 2: [1,2,5] sums to eight and is recorded.

Step 3: [2,6] sums to eight and is recorded.

Step 4: [1,1,6] sums to eight and is recorded, using both distinct physical ones.

Step 5: The second one at the same level is skipped where it would duplicate [1,7], so no duplicate sets appear.

```text
2026-10-27T00:10:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Coupon Redemption Planner (Combination Sum II)
2026-10-27T00:10:00Z [INFO] Found 4 redemption sets for target 8
2026-10-27T00:10:00Z [INFO] Set: [1, 1, 6]
2026-10-27T00:10:00Z [INFO] Set: [1, 2, 5]
2026-10-27T00:10:00Z [INFO] Set: [1, 7]
2026-10-27T00:10:00Z [INFO] Set: [2, 6]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  sort [1,1,2,5,6,7,10], target=8
    i+1 → use once ; skip i>start && cand[i]==cand[i-1]
      [1,1,6] [1,2,5] [1,7] [2,6]
    duplicate [1,7] via 2nd '1' at same level → pruned
  unique sets = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum II differs from the first version in two ways: each candidate may be used at most once, and the input can contain duplicates that must not produce duplicate combinations. I sort the candidates so equal values are adjacent, and in the recursion I advance the start index by one after choosing an element, which enforces the use-once rule. To suppress duplicate combinations I skip any element whose index is beyond the current level's start and that equals the previous element, which is the same same-level-duplicate guard I use in Subsets II.

The remaining-target logic is unchanged: I record when it reaches zero, abandon the branch when it goes negative, and because the array is sorted I break out of the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target to prune aggressively.

In my project at National Bank of India, a customer's wallet held one-time cashback coupons, some with identical values, and the system needed every distinct set of coupons that redeemed to an exact target. This use-once-plus-skip-duplicate template produced each valid set exactly once, which is the canonical recipe for collecting from a multiset without reuse.
